objectives: Spot techniques in a piece of writing.
Use techniques in your own sentences.
Plan and write a short persuasive piece for a clear reader.

keyVocabulary.meaning: to make someone agree with you or do something
the person or people you are writing for
the reason you are writing (here: to persuade)
a tool a writer uses, like a rhetorical question
a question to make the reader think (no answer needed)
words chosen to make the reader feel something
three points in a row for power (the rule of three)
a believable number used as evidence

techniques.meaning: words near each other start with the same sound
true information that is hard to argue with
techniques.example: Exercise is good for your heart.

techniques.meaning: what you believe, said with confidence
techniques.example: This is the best choice for everyone.

techniques.meaning: a question that makes the reader think
words that make the reader feel something
believable numbers that back you up
three points in a row for power

content.title: Remember (techniques)
lines: AFOREST = Alliteration, Facts, Opinion, Rhetorical question, Emotive language, Statistics, Triplet.
Use the technique — don't just name it.
2–3 strong techniques beat ten weak ones.

method.title: How to structure a persuasive piece
lines: 1  Hook — grab the reader (question, picture, bold line).
2  Point — make one clear point per paragraph.
3  Proof — back it up (fact, statistic or example).
4  Punch — end with a strong, emotive line.

model.title: Model paragraph (annotated)
model.text: Picture this: it is 1:15 and you have just five minutes left to eat. Is that really fair? A longer lunch would give us time to eat, move and reset. Over half of students say they feel rushed. We are tired, we are hungry, and we deserve better.

commonMistakes: Naming a technique instead of using it. Don't write 'I will use emotive language' — show it: 'Imagine losing everything you love.'
Making up silly statistics. Keep them believable, e.g. 'Over half of students…' not '100% of everyone ever.'
One giant paragraph. Use short paragraphs — one point each.
Forgetting your reader. Match your tone to the audience (a head teacher is different from a friend).

tasks.prompt:
Name the technique in each line:
(a) 'We must act now, now, now!'
(b) 'Is this the future we want?'
Match each technique to its meaning: Rhetorical question · Triplet · Statistic. (Write them next to the correct meaning.)
Rewrite this plain sentence to be persuasive. Use emotive language: 'The park is closing next month.'
Write a strong opening (hook) for a speech about why your school should recycle more. Use a rhetorical question.
Write a full persuasive paragraph (4–6 sentences) arguing for a longer lunch break. Use the structure: Hook → Point → Proof → Punch, and at least three techniques. Underline each technique you use.
